claims.text: A data-driven conductivity model incorporating microstructural defects and oxygen effects will be more accurate for bulk HfNbTaTiZr than conventional perfect-crystal analytical models.
The accuracy advantage will hold in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K temperature regimes.
Bulk HfNbTaTiZr can be synthesized through powder metallurgy or SPS involving gas-atomized powders.
The proposed sample set includes a very-low-oxygen HfNbTaTiZr specimen and a specimen intentionally containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The model will incorporate grain-boundary networks, dislocation densities, and oxygen-induced lattice distortions as predictive parameters.
The model will use inputs derived from ab initio data and active-learning strategies.
Conductivity measurements exist or will be performed at 0–200 K and 300–1200 K on HfNbTaTiZr samples with and without approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Quantum and scattering effects are prominent in the 0–200 K regime.
Grain boundaries, defect densities, and oxygen-related defect complexes modulate electron scattering and therefore conductivity.
Oxygen impurities and processing-induced defects cause local lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Local lattice distortions alter electron-scattering rates and carrier mobility.
Explicitly representing defect and oxygen effects overcomes the accuracy limitations of defect-free-crystal models.
The enhanced model will predict lower temperature sensitivity of conductivity due to defect-induced scattering.
The enhanced model will agree with measurements of oxygen-containing specimens better than traditional models.
Existing analytical conductivity predictions use perfect, defect-free hcp or bcc crystal approximations and inadequately represent real defects and oxygen impurities.
The model is applicable to similarly processed bulk HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen contents up to approximately 1 wt.%.
Predictions may deviate above 1200 K because of additional phase instabilities.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant accuracy improvement over traditional models, or failure to observe the predicted oxygen and defect sensitivity, would falsify the hypothesis.
